title: Police officers testify about shooting axe-wielding man
article: Two city police officers testified on Tuesday how they had to draw their guns and fire when they were met at the door of a northeast home by an axe-wielding man coming towards them on Oct. 20, 2011.

Const. Dave Thomas told the fatality inquiry that he and Const. Nathan Edwards were summoned to a domestic disturbance at the Citadel home about 10 p.m. but, en route, were advised the assailant, Peter Spiewak, was schizophrenic and may be armed with a knife and took precautions to protect him, themselves and the man's family inside.
Thomas said they planned to apprehend the man under the Mental Health Act, but just seconds after the door opened, were confronted with the man holding an axe.

"He had a look on his face, with his chin tucked in down to his chest," Thomas told inquiry counsel Neil Boyle. "I thought he zoomed in on me. My initial thought was I'm going to get killed. I drew my sidearm, raised it as a I backed up, and everything went black. I heard numerous shots, then it went silent."

Thomas realized later when he regained consciousness that he had tripped over a brick border around a flower garden near the front steps to the house and struck his head on a rock, sustaining a concussion. He did not realize until later at the district office that he had fired his handgun once and did not recall re-holstering his weapon.
Altogether, six shots were fired and Spiewak, 32, died at the scene.
Both officers were cleared of any wrongdoing, Alberta Serious Incident Response team lead investigator Al Brown testified on Monday.

Edwards, who fired five shots, testified that he was surprised when he saw Spiewak with what he believed was a fireman's axe above his shoulder, instead of a knife. He said the assailant was "zeroed in and focused on" his partner.
"An axe can kill you, no matter where it hits you, even in the leg," Edwards testified.
He said there was no option but to use lethal force, rather than physical force, for the preservation of himself, his partner and the deceased's family members.
"You never try to restrain somebody with your hands," Edwards said. "That's something you see in the movies."

Edwards said Thomas reached for his pistol and he heard a shot go off. He said he doesn't remember drawing his firearm, but remembers it being in his hand. He said he pulled the trigger, but doesn't recall if the shot hit Spiewak.
"I saw other family members coming to the door and Const. Thomas fell. If family members came out they could run in front of my pistol," he said. "I shot until I saw Mr. Spiewak slump to the ground."

Earlier, Richard Spiewak - Peter's father - testified that his daughter had come home with a friend that evening and the friend needed to remove her top so she could have some treatment and he asked Peter to leave the room and go upstairs for her privacy.
Peter became angry that he was being banished and an altercation ensued, he said.
"We sort of pushed each other," he said. "His sister pushed him. She pushed him back and she fell backwards and hit a table with a vase. I pushed Peter to some extent - to just help restore peace."
He said he believed his daughter called police.
It was then, he told police shortly afterwards, that Peter indicated he'd get a knife but his mother had hidden all of the knives.
Richard Spiewak said he was upstairs when he heard the doorbell ring several minutes later, then heard gunshots.
He ran downstairs and went outside, where he saw Peter had been killed and was on the ground.
The inquiry before provincial court Judge Gord Wong continues on Wednesday.
